title: Patton attacks in the rain

facts.text: On 8 November 1944, Lt. Gen. George S. Patton's Third Army opened a new offensive in Lorraine, aimed at Metz and the German border.
The weather was so bad that Maj. Gen. Manton Eddy, commanding XII Corps, asked Patton to postpone. Patton told him to attack as scheduled or name his successor.
The Germans thought the weather was too bad for an attack, so the assault caught them by surprise.
XII Corps opened with the biggest artillery preparation in Third Army history: 42 battalions and 540 guns fired 22,000 rounds.
Early on 9 November, the 90th Infantry Division crossed the swollen Moselle River at Koenigsmacker, north of Metz, and set up a secure bridgehead.
Because the water ran so high and fast, five days passed before armor could cross the Moselle there in force.
Seven inches of rain fell in Lorraine that November, about twice the normal amount, with rain on 20 days. It was the region's worst flooding in 35 years.
Mud and cloud cost the Americans much of their air advantage, and there was no air activity at all on 12 days of the month.
Trench foot put almost as many men out of action that month as enemy fire.

Army Signal Corps cameramen filmed the offensive on 9 November near Delme: shells bursting on German positions, tanks and infantry moving up, and men of the 35th Infantry Division searching German prisoners.
Third Army closed the ring around Metz on 19 November, and fighting in the city ended on 22 November, though the last of its forts held out until 13 December.
The Lorraine campaign cost Third Army 55,182 combat casualties.

sources.title: Christopher R. Gabel, The Lorraine Campaign: An Overview, September to December 1944, Combat Studies Institute, U.S. Army Command and General Staff College, 1985
New Offensive, Delme (111-ADC-2678) and shot card, U.S. National Archives

photoNote: Jeeps drive through the wrecked town of Dieuze, Lorraine, with troops of the 4th Armored Division on their way to the front, November 1944. U.S. Army photo printed on page 455 of the official history, The Lorraine Campaign (U.S. Army Center of Military History), public domain (via Wikimedia Commons; original 1176 px, downloaded at 1920 px so slightly soft). Dieuze fell later in the November offensive, so this is not 9 November itself; the caption should say November 1944. Muddy road and ruins fit the story.
photoCredit: Jeeps of the 4th Armored Division drive through the ruins of Dieuze, Lorraine, November 1944. U.S. Army photo, from The Lorraine Campaign (U.S. Army Center of Military History), public domain.

declassified.fact: Part of the blame for all that trench foot fell on supply officers in Europe. The quartermaster had declined to order a new winter uniform because he expected the war to be over before the cold came, and the troops in Lorraine fought the November rains without it.

A German officer captured when Metz fell, 22 November 1944. U.S. Air Force photo, NARA 342-FH-3A17757, public domain.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Army Signal Corps film, story LIB 537 'New Offensive', shot card dated 9 Nov 44 (silent). The card spells the place 'Delmen, Germany'; it is Delme, Moselle, France, in the XII Corps sector. The file is the stretch from 3:20 to 7:30 of the NARA reel, re-encoded at 30 fps. File times (checked on a contact sheet of the file): 0:00 to 0:04 the tail of the previous story, a dead German soldier in the Alps, leave it out; 0:05 to 0:20 tanks and vehicles move along a tree lined road, the best moving opener (a tank close at about 0:10 to 0:15); 0:25 a GI fires a machine gun; 0:30 to 0:40 an infantry column moves up the road; 0:45 to 1:05 men of the 35th Division search German prisoners; 1:10 to 1:20 prisoners walk down a village street; 1:25 a surrender leaflet; 1:35 to 2:10 a burned out U.S. truck and tank retriever; 2:15 onward more prisoners. The reel's next story, first snow at Houffalize on 10 Nov, is not in the file.
film.license: U.S. Army Signal Corps film, U.S. government work, public domain (NARA's blanket 'possibly copyright' flag on 111-ADC reels)
film.date_note: Filmed 9 November 1944 in the XII Corps sector south of Metz; the Moselle crossing at Koenigsmacker in the facts was north of Metz, so the caption should not say the film shows the river crossing.
